extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interpreting and evaluating patent claims during prosecution, including assessing asserted utility, applying the broadest reasonable interpretation, plain meaning, lexicography/disavowal, means‑plus‑function, and the effect of preambles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility of asserted utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner must determine whether an asserted utility is credible based on the information disclosed in the application; absence of a known cure is not a basis to conclude lack of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only claims for which an asserted utility is not credible should be rejected. Credibility is judged from the specification and supporting evidence; modest evidence may suffice to support a claim of treating a symptom, while claims of 'curing' a disease require significantly greater evidentiary support. Expert affidavits indicating a reasonable expectation of success, supported by sound reasoning (e.g., in light of FDA clinical-trial practices), usually suffice to establish credibility. Cite case law examples (In re Jolles, In re Sichert, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, pending claims must be given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI is applied by the PTO (not the same as court claim construction) to the claim language as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art, taking into account the specification. The standard reduces the chance that issued claims will be interpreted more broadly than justified because applicants can amend during prosecution. BRI does not mean the broadest possible interpretation; the construction must be consistent with ordinary and customary meaning and the specification. Relevant authorities and rule citations (Phillips, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Words of a claim given plain (ordinary and customary) meaning unless inconsistent with the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, claim words are given their plain meaning (ordinary and customary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention), unless the specification rebuts that meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ordinary meaning may be evidenced by claims, specification, drawings, and prior art, but the specification is the best source—ideally serving as a glossary. If the specification clearly sets a different definition, that special definition controls. Examples (Chef America, In re Zletz) illustrate applying plain meaning and when to follow a spec-defined meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import limitations from the specification into the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to read limitations from a particular embodiment in the written description into a claim when the claim language is broader than that embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the written description may aid understanding, examiners must avoid narrowing claims by importing unrecited limitations. Exceptions include when claim language invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (means-plus-function), in which case the specification must be consulted to determine corresponding structure, material, or acts and the claim is limited to those equivalents. Case examples (Superguide, Liebel‑Flarsheim, In re Donaldson, In re Marosi, Zletz) illustrate improper importing and proper limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑plus‑function (35 U.S.C. 112(f)/pre‑AIA 112, 6th para.) construal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim element is expressed as means- or step-plus-function, the specification must be consulted to identify corresponding structure, material, or acts, and the element is limited to what is described and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim language falls under 112(f), examiners must construe the element in light of the specification’s disclosure of structure/acts/materials. This construal limits the claim to the corresponding disclosure and equivalents. Cite In re Donaldson and MPEP §§ 2181–2186 for procedure and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for determining ordinary and customary meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary and customary meaning of a claim term may be evidenced by claims themselves, specification, drawings, prior art, and dictionaries; the specification is preferred when clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification clearly defines a term, extrinsic evidence is unnecessary. If ambiguity remains or no ordinary meaning exists, examiners should look to specification and prior art; if no reasonably clear meaning can be ascribed, apply the broadest reasonable interpretation and consider a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection and spec objections under 37 CFR 1.75(d). Case examples include Vitronics, In re Abbott Diabetes Care, and In re Suitco Surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant as lexicographer (special definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may rebut the presumption of ordinary meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of a claim term in the specification; such lexicography must be deliberate and sufficiently clear to give notice to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification provides an explicit definition, that definition controls claim interpretation. The special meaning must be sufficiently clear and deliberate (In re Paulsen, Intellicall). If a special meaning is present, the examiner should acknowledge and identify it on the record. Examples (Toro Co., Old Town Canoe) show where spec definitions govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disavowal of claim scope (clear and unmistakable disclaimer)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may narrow the presumed ordinary meaning by clearly disavowing or disclaiming claim scope in the specification, but disavowal must be clear and unmistakable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disavowal can be explicit or, in some cases, implicit where the specification consistently excludes or disparages a feature across all embodiments. If the examiner believes implicit disavowal narrows BRI, the examiner should make that interpretation clear on the record. Examples (SciMed, In re Am. Acad. of Sci. Tech. Ctr., In re Abbott Diabetes Care) illustrate explicit and implicit disavowal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of the preamble on claim scope (structural vs. purpose/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim preamble limits the claim is a case‑by‑case determination based on the entire record; a preamble that recites structural limitations or is necessary to give life and meaning to the claim is limiting, whereas a mere statement of purpose or intended use is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should review the entire application to determine if preamble language limits structure or merely states purpose. If the body of the claim sets forth all limitations and the preamble only states intended use, the preamble is not a limitation (Pitney Bowes, Rowe v. Dror). However, if the preamble provides structural limitations or the intended use results in a structural/manipulative difference over prior art, the preamble limits the claim (Corning, Kropa, Jansen, In re Cruciferous Sprout Litig.). Evaluate whether prior art capable of performing the recited purpose meets the claim. Use cited cases and hypothetical examples to guide analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner decision flow for terms not invoking 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: A stepwise process examiners should follow to determine claim term meaning under BRI when 112(f) is not invoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Determine if the term has an ordinary and customary meaning to one of ordinary skill. 2a) If yes, check the specification for a special definition. 2b) If the spec provides a special definition, use it and identify it in the Office action. 2c) If not, apply the ordinary meaning. 3) If no ordinary meaning exists, check the specification for a meaning; if none can be reasonably ascribed after considering spec and prior art, apply BRI as best understood and reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d). Office actions should acknowledge any special definition when used.
